name: Investment Committee Memos
title: Investment Committee Memos
answer: Investment committee memos are the formal documents that present a proposed investment to the committee that approves, rejects, or conditions it. In an agent workflow, the memo is not just a static write-up but the assembled record of data pulls, model outputs, diligence notes, and risk flags that an analyst or agent prepares for review. For AI-related strategies, the evidence base can include 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices, 355 merger and acquisition filings, 432 company pages, 148 active AI lawsuits, and 219 compliance and regulation pages. The scope covers public equities, private deals, funds, and other instruments, depending on the mandate. The memo must state the thesis, the valuation, the risks, and the recommendation in a form the committee can challenge.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Agent workflows for investment committee memos run on a stack that combines market data feeds, document stores, and workflow orchestration. The data layer may include daily prices for listed instruments, merger and acquisition filings, company pages, litigation records, and compliance and regulation pages. The agent layer uses large language models and retrieval tools to draft sections, summarize filings, and check consistency against source documents. The workflow layer tracks versions, approvals, and audit logs so that every number and claim can be traced back to a source. Access controls and data residency rules determine which agents and analysts can see which deal materials.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The process usually starts with a request or a deal trigger, and then an agent gathers the relevant filings, market data, and internal notes. The agent drafts sections such as the executive summary, investment thesis, valuation, risks, and diligence findings, and it flags gaps for human review. A human analyst or committee secretary then edits, verifies, and resolves conflicts before the memo is circulated. Agents can also run consistency checks, compare the memo against prior committee decisions, and produce a redline for reviewers. The final memo is a human-approved document, even when agents did most of the assembly.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance is central because committee memos influence capital allocation and must be defensible under audit and regulatory review. Each data point, model output, and agent action should carry a source, a timestamp, and a version, so the committee can see what was known and when. Rights and permissions matter for licensed market data, confidential deal materials, and personal data, and agents must respect those limits. Risk includes hallucinated figures, stale prices, missed litigation, and overreliance on a single model, so human review and source checks are standard controls. The memo should also disclose the role of AI agents in its preparation, because governance policies and regulators increasingly expect that transparency.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Agent workflows for investment committee memos are moving toward tighter integration with portfolio systems, so a memo can update as prices, filings, or risk signals change. The trend points to more automated evidence gathering, more structured data extraction from filings and contracts, and more real-time compliance checks. The human committee will likely keep the decision rights, while agents handle preparation, monitoring, and post-decision reporting. Evaluation will focus on traceability, accuracy, and whether the memo surfaces the same risks a skilled analyst would find. As regulation and litigation around AI continue to develop, the memo format may evolve to include standard AI-use disclosures and model risk assessments.
